abstract.p: Land can be put into different uses with little consideration of attendant effects on human health and environment. This study aimed to assess the levels of natural radioactivity (40K, 226Ra and 232Th) and associated radiological hazards in soil samples from selected land use types in parts of Abeokuta metropolis, southwest Nigeria. A total of thirty (30) composite surface (0–30 cm) soil samples from six (6) different land uses—abattoir waste site (ABT), cement block making site (BMS), textile dye-contaminated site (DCS), automobile mechanic village site (MVS), welding & fabrication site (W&FS) and grassland (GLS) were collected and determined for activity concentration (AC) of natural radionuclides using NaI (Tl) scintillation detector. Radiological hazard indices (RHI) were later calculated using established UNSCEAR relations. The results of soil natural radioactivity levels revealed that the average ACs of 226Ra (57.66 ± 33.48–156.67 ± 48.78 Bq/kg) and 232Th (131.68 ± 41.10–213.96 ± 45.00 Bq/kg) in all investigated land uses were higher than their corresponding global mean values of 39 and 45 Bq/kg, correspondingly. The soils from all selected land uses had average AC of 40K (206.34 ± 69.98–316.68 ± 67.54 Bq/kg) below the weighted world average value of 420 Bq/kg. Average values of RHI such as annual dose rate (118.90–196.39 nGyhr−1), outdoor annual effective dose equivalent (145.82–240.86 μSv/yr), annual gonadal dose equivalent (821.28–1350.53 μSv/yr), gamma level index (1.89–3.09) and activity utilization index (2.21–3.69) of soils in all selected land uses were above the global average standards. Excess lifetime cancer risk values ranged from 0.51 to 0.84 × 10−3, exceeding the global average of 0.29 × 10−3. Multivariate statistics revealed that 232Th is the primary contributor to the radiological hazard. This study revealed considerable radiological risks from natural radionuclides in the topsoils of investigated land use types.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Soil plays a crucial role in supporting comfort of human beings existence through the provision of land for growing of crops, provision of habitat, setting up of workplaces for agro and commercial-based industries among others1–4. The levels of natural occurring radionuclides in environmental media vary from one place to another as this depends on geographical positioning, pedogenic processes, geological settings, nature of radiochemical present, prevailing geochemical process, human activities etc.4–7. Human beings engage in various daily activities that mostly take place on land surface/soil. Soil serves as principal exposure medium of natural radioactivity that permits unrestricted transfer of radionuclides into the surroundings8. Soil not just acts as an origin of continual radioactivity contact to human beings, moreover as an effective medium of relocation for the transport of radio-elements to biosystems4,9.

Activities that encourage release of contaminants or waste water to the immediate environment presumably pose environmental threats (human and ecological health risks) which negatively affect preservation of fragile ecosystem. According to10,11, uncurbed industrial and human activities have led to enhanced levels of contaminants such as potentially toxic elements, volatile organic compounds and radionuclides in soil together with their associated long-time cumulative health effects. Soil is one of the raw materials used in manufacturing of bricks and concrete blocks which serve as one of the major building materials for construction purpose. Therefore, cement block making site can also acts as potential source of external and internal radiation exposure to artisans working on the site12,13. Textile dyes of different types, used in textile industry are one of the persistent environmental pollutants that threaten quality of water bodies and soil14,15. Complexed metal dye harbors some potentially toxic elements while azo-type dyes (synthetic dyes) that were non-binding to the fabric during the dyeing process, generate wastewater that pollute soil matrix16,17. Abattoir sites are consistent source of natural radionuclides18. Animals slaughtered in abattoir sites have usually grazed over extensive areas and, through their ingestion of grasses and soil may accumulate radionuclides in their tissues, eventually passed into abattoir wastes such as blood and dung18,19.

Many hazardous substances and aerosols, which contributes to various acute and chronic health challenges are released into the environment during welding and fabrication activities20. Although, majority of potential health risks associated with welding activities have been attributed to welding fumes and non-ionizing radiation20–22. Ndoma et al.20 and Antonini23 however, highlighted remarkable similarity in some respiratory challenges caused by welding fumes and those associated with ionizing radiation from gamma-ray emissions.

Automobile maintenance and repairing activities are other land use of concern. In Nigeria government usually allocate a wide expense of land commonly known as mechanic village to automobile technicians (mechanics), electricians (rewirers), panel beaters, spray painters etc. to offer different repairs and maintenance services to vehicle users11,24. There is inevitable presence of spent engine oils, lubricants, petroleum solvents and paints on automobile mechanic work sites6,11. The oil-contaminated soils at mechanics village pose environment threat to soil and nearby shallow aquifer units11,24. It is therefore essential to evaluate the concentrations of natural radionuclides in the aforementioned contaminated soils.

In this research, the natural radioactivity concentrations in the soil samples of abattoir, cement block making site, welding and fabrication site, automobile mechanic, textile making site and grassland soil in parts of Abeokuta metropolis, Ogun State Nigeria will be determined through gamma ray spectrometry. This study can be considered as baseline study for future evaluation of the radiological impacts of different land use activities on human beings and the environment. This study provides information of public relevance, particularly for local artisans and workers, by increasing awareness of potential radiological risks associated with soil radionuclide concentrations.

sec.title: Description of selected land use patterns
sec.p:
Six land use patterns were considered. These are abattoir waste site (ABT), welding and fabrication site (W&FS), textile dye-contaminated site (DCS), cement block making site (BMS), automobile mechanic village site (MVS) and grassland (GLS) (Fig. 1). The ABT and BMS have been in existence since early 2010. The DCS and W&FS have been in existence since early 2010 and 2015, respectively. The MVS has been in existence since 1999.Fig. 1
Geological map of the research site (adopted from25).

sec.title: Soil samples collection
sec.p: For this study, five representative soil samples were collected at each land use. Therefore, a total of thirty (30) clusters soil samples were collected from selected six land use types on the same lithology (basement complex formation).

The sampling at each land use type was planned in such a pattern that soil sample (at a depth of 30 cm using a soil anger) was picked in a rectangular lattice of 5 m by 2 m, created with the help of a tape measure11. Five different sampling points were created within the grid: four samples were collected at each of the corners of the grid and one at the centre of the grid, making a total of five (5) clusters, which were then mixed to form a representative sample.

sec.title: Sample preparation
sec.p: The collected samples were dried at room temperature for 2 days, after being crushed to particle sizes of < 0.2 mm. Thereafter, soil samples were withered at 105 °C for 24 h so as to eliminate moistness content, and then pulverized into powder to obtain homogeneous sample26,27.

About 400 g each of the homogenized sample was put in a cylindrical plastic container, carefully sealed and kept in the laboratory for 28 days so as to allow 226Ra and its progenies to reach secular equilibrium prior to gamma-ray spectrometry27,28.

sec.title: Radiometric analysis
Radiometric data treatment
sec.p: Statistical analysis employed in the study includes simple descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, cluster analysis (CA) and principal component analysis (PCA). All the statistical analyses were performed using statistical software package SPSS version 20.0. The average values of measured natural radionuclides in soil samples for each land use type were compared with global average acceptable values and published studies on soil natural radioactivity. Pearson’s Correlation Analysis was carried out on the radiometric data to identify relationships between measured natural radionuclides and associated RHI. The CA was performed in accordance with agglomerative schedule where a blend of Ward’s Linkage and Squared Euclidean distances were used to measure the similarity or dissimilarity between analyzed natural radionuclides and/or sampling points27,32,38. Ward’s method was used because it looked for clusters in multivariate Euclidean space and also produced groups that minimize within-group dispersion at each binary fusion38–40. On the other hand, PCA was employed to identify significant properties/parameters that explain most of the variations of the initial data set27,37. PCA extracts component with eigenvalue greater than unity which described more aggregate variant in the data. Sole component with eigenvalue greater than 1 were recalled and thereafter exposed to varimax rotation41,42. Both HCA and PCA were used to infer the probable sources of natural radionuclides27,36.

sec.title: Positive matrix factorization model
sec.p: To accomplish this aim, the resolving algorithm of the PMF concurrently changed the elements of gik and fkj in each iterative-least square technique till global lowest is reached. In this work, the uncertainty matrix uij was obtained utilizing equation based approached47. A 12 × 31 matrices of activity concentration and uncertainty of radionuclides and radiological indices were then uploaded into United States Environmental Protection Agency Positive Matrix Factorization (USEPA PMF 5.0) software. A 3 factors was chosen for combined activity concentrations and radiological indices according to satisfactory fitness of the data with the good concurrence between the predicted and input elemental concentrations data and for meaningful factor profiles and contributions.

Higher values of 226Ra > 100 Bq/kg were recorded in ABT, DCS, W&FS and GLS. Lower AC of 226Ra < 100Bq/kg were recorded in both MVS (57.66 ± 33.48) and BMS (64.48 ± 41.40 Bg/kg). Comparatively higher values of 226Ra were recorded in trio of ABT, DCS and W&FS than that of GLS (Table 2). Highest 226Ra in ABT soil could be due to its higher organic matter content49–51.

The mean AC of 232Th are 131.68 ± 41.1Bq/kg (in BMS); 171.88 ± 63.73 Bq/kg (in ABT); 189.10 ± 50.00 Bq/kg (in DCS); 202.04 ± 38.02 Bq/kg (in GLS); 198.87 ± 27.94Bq/kg (in W&FS) and 213.96 ± 45.00Bq/kg (in MVS).

The highest and lowest AC of 232Th were recorded in MVS and BMS, respectively. Maximum average AC of 232Th in MVS could be due to inherent existence of potentially toxic elements and naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) in spent engine oil52,53. Furthermore, the AC of 232Th in all investigated land uses were above the global average of 45 Bq/kg recommended by UNSCEAR48. This is an indication of presence of thorium bearing minerals present in the soils of the study area54,55.

In the case of 40K, its AC in collected soil samples ranged from 206.34 ± 69.98Bq/Kg (in W&FS) to 316.68 ± 67.54 Bq/Kg (in DCS) and all lie below the world average of 420 Bq/kg48. Higher average value of 40K (> 280 Bq/kg) was recorded in dye-contaminated soil (DCS) relative to its values (< 280 Bq/kg) in other sites, but still lower than the world average value in soil which is 420 Bq/kg.

Higher ACs of 226Ra and 40K in DCS might be due to prevalence of dispersive dyes as well as presence of textile dye compounds/manufacturing additives such as titanium dioxide, zirconium compounds, metal-complex dyes and mordants in DCS17.

The average AC values of 232Th greater than that of 226Ra in samples from each of the selected land uses concurs with report of World Nuclear Association56. In addition, higher concentration of 232Th relative to 226Ra in each of the investigated land uses might be because it sticks more to the soil than 226Ra55.

It should be noted that enriched levels of 226Ra and 232Th in soil samples for all the investigated land use patterns indicate presence of monazite and zircus content in soil of the study area57. Range of values of activity concentrations of 40K, 226Ra and 232Th detected in soils of the selected land uses might be due to granitic lithology of the study area58.

The order of abundance of the activity concentrations of tested natural radionuclides in the soils of all selected land uses follows: 40K > 232Th > 226Ra. Similar observation has been reported by Jegede et al.28 and Muhammad et al.59. The pattern of the radionuclide distribution among the six (6) selected land uses fit perfectly into the overall order, indicating that the soil type of each land use might be derived from the same geological background60.

This distribution pattern is however in contrast to 40K > 226Ra > 232Th and 232Th > 226Ra > 40K obtained by Olaoye et al.6 and Ilori and Alausa61, respectively, who measured ACs of natural radionuclides in cattle dung–laden soil and automobile oil contaminated soil, respectively.

Specifically, the order of natural radionuclides in BMS soil for this study concurs with 40K > 232 Th > 226Ra in quarry soil from Odeda, Abeokuta, Nigeria and in granitic soil from Ilorin, Nigeria by Jegede et al.28 and Orosun et al.62, respectively.

Figure 2 illustrates the box plots of the distributions of 40K, 226Ra and 232Th in soil samples across the study areas. From Fig. 2, it can be seen that 40K exhibited the most variation levels in ABT and MVS; 226Ra demonstrated strong enrichment in ABT and DCS while there is persistently elevated 232Th activity concentrations throughout MVS and W&FS sites. BMS group displayed the lowest level of variability for all radionuclide measurement across the whole studied land uses.Fig. 2

sec.p:

The average ADR (in nGyhr−1) due to contaminated soils of investigated land uses ranged between 118.90 (in BMS) and 196.39 nGyhr−1 (in DCS). The mean ADR values in all land uses were above the worldwide average of 59 nGyh−148. The trend of ADR values follows the order: ADR in DCS > ADR in W&FS > ADR in ABT > ADR in GLS > ADR in MVS > ADR in BMS. For the AEDE outdoor values, it ranges from 145.82 (in BMS) to 240.86 μSv/yr (in DCS). All the AEDEoutdoor values in selected land uses are above the acceptable world average value of 70 µSv/yr48. The gonads and the bone marrow cells are regarded as the sensitive parts of human body in radiological studies48. Therefore, average AGDE values in the soil samples from all investigated land use patterns were above the global average of 300 µSv/yr (Table 3).

Minimum and maximum values of AGDE were recorded in the soils of BMS and DCS, respectively. The average internal and external hazard indices (Hin & Hext) values in BMS soil (0.91 and 0.73) were < 1.00 while their values in remaining land uses were above the acceptable value (1.00)48. The representative gamma index (Iy) values for all the soil samples were greater than the admissible value of 1.00 stipulated by UNSCEAR48 (Table 3). Highest and lowest values of Iy were recorded in DCS and BMS, respectively (Table 3). In the case of AUI, its mean values for all the land uses vary from 2.21 (in BMS) to 3.69 (in DCS) (Table 3). It was observed that the AUI values for the selected land uses were above the global acceptable average value of 2.0048. This is an indication that majority of the soils in the selected land uses are not radiologically safe for use as building material63.

The values of alpha index (Iα) of all the soil samples were lower than the recommended limit value of 1.0048. The average ELCR values in soil samples ranged from 0.51 × 10–3 (inn BMS soil) to 0.84 × 10–3 (in DCS). The average values of ELCR for all investigated land uses were above the worldwide average limit of 0.29 × 10–3. This indicates higher probability of developing carcinogenic risks over the generation span of artisans and users of these land use patterns in the study location.

Comparison of the values of RHI obtained in this study with similar/related published works show remarkable outcomes. The values of RHI obtained in MVS with similar oil-contaminated sites reveal that ranges of ADR, Hext, AGDE and Raeq in this research were greater than those documented by Olaoye et al.6 and Aruna et al.24. Nevertheless, average values of ADR and AGDE (63.73 nGyhr−1 and 428.22 µSv/yr reported by Adebiyi and Ore9 in oil-contaminated soil were also above the international standard reference values, as obtained in the present study. Olaoye et al.6 also reported ADR (79.00 nGyhr−1) higher than the acceptable limit of 59 nGyhr−1. However, Aruna et al.24, in similar oil-contaminated soils at mechanic workshops in Ibadan (Southwest, Nigeria) reported values of computed RHI lower than permissible world average values. The likely reasons for the relatively higher values of radiological indices in studied MVS compared to that of6,9,24 could be attributed to high levels of vehicles repairing and maintenance activities by various pool of artisans in the mechanic village, differences in geological background and types of metals scraps used by the automobile technicians6,9.
Results of RHI in MV soils is an indication that long-time exposure to radionuclides from the MVS soils may enhance chances of radiological hazards to the artisans working in the MV.

All the computed radiological indices except alpha index (Iα) in W&FS had higher values above the permissible global threshold values set by UNSCEAR48. Ndoma et al.20 also reported that some welding locations have ADR, AEDEoutdoor, AGDE and ELCR values above the allowable limits stipulated by UNSCEAR48. For ABT soil, values of most of the estimated RHI gotten in this research were comparatively greater than Raeq (124.03 Bq/kg), ADR (108.78 nGyhr−1), AUI (0.80) and Iy (0.92) reported by Jibiri et al.18 in abattoir sediments in some parts of southwest Nigeria. However, AEDEoutdoor in ABT soil (228.26 µSv/yr) for this study was lower than the reported mean AEDEoutdoor of 533.65 µSv/yr by Jibiri et al.18.

The average values of ADR, AEDEoutdoor, ELCR, AGDE, Iy, and AUI in BMS were above the permissible world averages recommended by UNSCEAR48 (Table 3). This is in contrast to results of13 where only ADR has value (115 nGyhr−1) greater than allowable limit of 59 nGyhr−1. Similar higher ELCR, ADR and AGDE values above the permissible limits were also observed in four (4) types of different cement samples in Senegal by Ndour et al.35. The average Raeq (270.34 Bq/kg), Hext and Hin (< 1.0) in BMS soil were below the acceptable world average limits of 370Bq/kg, 1.00 and 1.00, respectively.

Remarkably, the average values of Raeq (270.34 Bq/kg), ADR (118.90 nGyh−1), Hin (0.91), Hext (0.73), AEDEoutdoor (145.82 µSvy−1), AGDE (821.88 µSvy−1), ELCR (0.51 × 10–3) and Iy (1.89) obtained in BMS soil for this study compare well with reported mean values of Raeq (282.22 Bq/kg), ADR (130.20 nGyh−1), Hin (0.86), Hext (0.76), AEDEoutdoor (159.78 µSvy−1), AGDE (923.36 µSvy−1), ELCR of 0.56 × 10–3 and gamma level index (Iy) of 1.05 in quarry soil samples from Odeda (the same locality/geographical setting of the present study location) by Jegede et al.28.

For textile dye-contaminated soil samples at DCS, the maximum values of all computed RHI except alpha index (Iα) were observed in DCS and lie above the international reference values. Higher mean values of radiological indices in DCS might be due to the use of different types of textile dyes in making of Kampala fabric (a popular locally made textile brand in Southwest Nigeria) in the study area. In fact, Abeokuta (in Ogun state, Nigeria) is regarded as the main hub of Kampala textile producers in the Country. Fouda et al.17 and Abdel Ghany and Ibrahim64 reported lower values of RHI that lie within the acceptable limits in textile dyes and dye-waste-water, respectively. Both of them highlighted unexpected radiation hazards in textile dyes.

Average ACs of 40K, 232Th, and 226Ra in soils from mechanic village workshops (MVS) were significantly higher than their corresponding values reported by Olaoye et al.6 and Adebiyi and Ore9 in similar oil-contaminated sites at Akure (Ondo State, Nigeria) and Ojo and Ijegun in Lagos, Nigeria, respectively (Table 4). The disparity in average concentrations of natural radioactivity in soils from MVS at Abeokuta (underlain by basement complex formation) and that of6,9 might be due to differences in level of activities in the study site, amount of spilled spent oil contaminants, geological settings and sample size9,24.

The mean values of 40K, 226Ra and 232Th in soil samples from W&FS for this study were quite different from their reported corresponding mean values of 336.22, 27.85 and 37.97Bq/kg, respectively by Ndoma et al.20 in similar welding and fabrication workshop in Akwa Ibom, South South Nigeria (Table 5). It should be noted that geological background, age of the site, differences in topographic conditions and work frequency of welding shops has impacts on the ACs of natural radionuclides20,55.

The mean values of tested natural radionuclides in BMS soil were compared with similar studies of natural radionuclides (226Ra, 232Th and 40K) with similar studies of natural radionuclides in cement samples from Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal, Poland as well as in quarry and granitic soils in Nigeria (Table 6).

The AC of 226Ra in BMS soil was relatively higher than its corresponding values in cement samples from Cote d’Ivoire & Poland (Table 6). This might be attributed to mixture of raw materials (cement, quarry dust, soil, fine and coarse aggregates) used in making of concrete blocks at the BMS as well as presence of fly ashes in cement used at the BMS13,68. The mean value of 40K in BMS soil was lower than its corresponding value in cement samples from Poland (283.00 Bq/kg) and 2056.44 Bq/kg in quarry soil from Odeda (the same locality with the present study area), Ogun State, Nigeria. The higher value of 40K in quarry soil by Jegede et al.28 might be due to the presence of micronutrients like Cu, Fe and Mn69. In addition, quarry soils are basically derived from a mixture of granitic igneous and sedimentary rocks, and they act as a source rock for naturally occurring radionuclide materials (NORM), hence the reason for the high AC of 40K in quarry soil28,70.

The AC of 40K in ABT soil for this study was lower than the mean value of 40K in soil form cattle dung disposal site at Mangoro-Agege (Lagos, Nigeria) (403.07 Bq/kg) by Ilori and Alausa61 (Table 7). Furthermore, the mean value of 40K in abattoir soil (ABT) obtained in this study was lower than the reported mean 40K of 290.04 Bq/kg in abattoir sediments around selected abattoir sites in Southwest Nigeria by Jibiri et al.18. However, the mean values of 226Ra and 232Th in ABT soils for this study were comparatively higher than their corresponding values in similar abattoir sites by Jibiri et al.18 and Ilori and Alausa61 (Table 7). The variations in the mean values of tested natural radionuclides in ABT soil for this study compared to that of Jibiri et al.18 and Ilori and Alausa61 might be because collected soil samples in this study were from a nearby dump that contains mixture of cow dungs, bone ash and blood. In addition, disparity in average values of natural radionuclides in ABT soil compared to previous similar studies might be due to differences in geological settings, nature of environmental media and composition of animal wastes in the soil sampling points (Table 7).

The mean AC of 40K in GLS for this study was lower than that of 40K in farmland soil near tin mining areas in Kano, North Central Nigeria and in maize farmland soil at Ayetoro, Ogun State (Soutwest Nigeria) by Muhammad et al.59 and Ofomola et al.67, respectively (Table 8). This could be attributed to the use of inorganic fertilizer at the farmlands, which adds up to the 40K-content in the soil4. However, higher values of 226Ra and 232Th in GLS for this present study were comparatively higher than mean values of 226Ra and 232Th (64.6 and 72.03 Bq/kg respectively) reported by Muhammad et al.59 in farmland soils near gold mining sites in Kano, Nigeria (Table 8).

The average concentrations of 226Ra, 40K and 232Th in DCS were compared with previous works of Abdel Ghany and Ibrahimv64 and Fouda et al.17 in dye and dye waste-water, respectively (Table 9). This is because there are no existing works on natural radionuclides in textile dye-polluted soils that could be applied to compare the soil’s radionuclide content of textile dye-contaminated soils for this study. The discrepancy in our results of ACs of tested natural radionuclides in DCS relative to that of64 and17 might be attributed to differences in raw materials used, manufacturing processes, specific types of textile dyes used, and environmental media, all of which can impact the radionuclide content17.

sec.title: Interpretation of Elemental concentration of Radionuclides
sec.p: Using the above categorization, mean eTh/eRa values in ABT, BMS, DCS, W&FS and GLS suggests soil underlain by poor weathering rock type while its value in MVS (13.65) suggests absence of favourable enrichment of uranium/radium, possibly due to more compaction of the MV soil. The Clark ratio (eTh/eRa) (13.65) obtained for MVS is relatively higher than its corresponding value (8.17) in a similar oil-contaminated site, at Ojo and Ijegun (Lagos, Nigeria) by Olaoye et al.6. All the average values of eTh/K in collected soil samples were significantly higher than the normal crustal value (for unaltered lithology) (0.003–0.005). This is an indication that sufficient reworking activities occurred in all the studied land uses74. Furthermore, higher values of eTh/K in the soil samples also implies non-hydrothermally altered zones characterized by thorium rich bearing minerals72,75.

sec.title: Correlation analysis
sec.p:
Table 11 presents the correlation coefficient matrix of measured radionuclides and associated radiological hazard and indices. From Table 11, weak negative relationship exists between 40K and 232Th (r = − 0.026). This is an indication of differences in geochemical behavior, mobility in soil, and sources of 40K and 232Th80,81. It could also be due to the fact that 40K does not belongs to the 226Ra and 232Th decay series32,37. It was also observed that weak correlation exists between 40K and estimated RHI. Similar weak correlation between 40K and estimated RHI was also reported by Senthilkumar and Narayanaswamy54 and Ogundele et al.82. Weak positive correlation exists between 226Ra and 232Th (r = 0.148). 226 Ra had good positive correlations with Hin and Iα (r > 0.800) and moderate positive correlations with most of the remaining RHI. Strong positive correlations between 232Th and most of the RHI indicate that 232Th was the significant contributor to the gaming radiation emission in the study site, closely followed by 226Ra. This could be an indication that a rise in the specific activity distribution of 232Th in the selected land use types could possibly leads to radiological health impacts36. Strong positive associations (r > 0.900) exist between Raeq and each of the remaining computed RHI except Iα (Table 11). Very strong positive correlations exist between ADR and each of ELCR and AEDEoutdoor (r = 1.000) as well as high good correlations (with r = 0.995–0.997) with the remaining RHI except Iα. Positive correlation between ADR and AEDEoutdoor was also reported by Imani et al.83. Very strong positive association exists between ELCR and AEDEoutdoor (r = 1.000). External hazard index (Hext) displays strong positive relationship with Iγ, AGDE, AUI, AEDEoutdoor, Hin and Iα with correlation coefficients that range from 0.958 to 1.000. Alpha index (Iα) exhibits moderate positive correlation (r = 0.502–0.532) with most of the RHI (Raeq, ELCR, ADR, Hext, AGDE, AUI and AEDEoutdoor) but weak correlations with 40K and 232Th. sec.title: Principal component analysis
sec.p:
The outcomes of PCA reveals that only two (2) components have their eigenvalues greater than unity (1.0) (Table 12). These two components accounted for 92.12% of the total variations in the data set. The principal component I (PCI) accounts for 79.90% of the total variation while the principal component 2 (PC2) accounts for 12.21% of the total variability. The second component (PC2) has moderate loading on 226Ra and Iα, weak positive loadings on 40K and Hin as well as negative loadings on other radiological parameters and 232Th. From the overall PCA, It can be summarized that 232Th and 226Ra contributed significantly to the estimation of RHI in the studied land uses. sec.title: Positive matrix factorization analysis results
sec.p:
Figure 5 displays the factor profiles resolved by PMF for the activity concentration and radiological indices The blue bars indicate the concentrations of the elements in the source profiles while the red square box in each bar denote the percentage explained variation for the element for that factor. The left Y-axis is a logarithmic scale correspond to concentration while the right Y- axis denotes the percentage of species. The first Factor contained 232Th, ADR, ELCR, AGDE, AEDE with 57.7%, 37.9%, 37.8 5% and 37.9% as the percentage explained variance Hence, the first factor is linked to Thorium source being the dominant radionuclide with highest contribution. The second factor was characterized by 226Ra, ADR, AGDE, AEDE and Iɣ with 80.0%, 29.3%, 28.0%, 29.3%, and 76.4% as the percentage explained variation. This factor is linked to Radium source due to the fact that Ra has the highest percentage contribution. The third factor exhibited high loading of 40K with 97.1%, as the percentage explained variation and it is associated to Potassium source.Fig. 5

sec.title: Cluster analysis results
sec.p:
From the hierarchical cluster analysis, three groups were identified (Fig. 6). These are Cluster 1 that contains 226Ra, 232Th, 40K, ADR, Hext, Hin, ELCR, AUI, AEDEoutdoor, Iγ and Iα. Cluster 2 contains only Raeq while Cluster 3 contains only AGDE. Cluster 1 indicated that natural radionuclides and the associated RHI belong to the same common components of terrestrial environments where naturally occurring radionuclide materials serve as the major contributors to natural background radiation82,84. Cluster 2 contains Raeq only, which is a radiological parameter that effectively provides a standardized benchmark to compare the combined hazard of 232Th, 40K and 226Ra using a common unit of Bq/kg36,85. Cluster 3 contains AGDE which is specifically related to dose received by gonads and bone marrow, due to their high radio sensitivity86.Fig. 6

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study assessed levels of natural radioactivity and associated radiological hazards arising from exposure to contaminated soils from selected land use types in parts of Abeokuta, Southwest Nigeria. The mean concentrations of 226Ra and 232Th in soil samples from all selected land uses were above the world average permissible limits of 39 and 45 Bq/kg, respectively. In addition, estimated mean values of ADR, AEDE outdoor, ELCR, Iγ and AUI were above the international reference values in all selected non-agricultural land uses. Among the studied land uses, the DCS and ABT pose the highest radiological risk and should be prioritized for regulatory monitoring and intervention. Multivariate statistical analysis revealed that 232Th is the primary contributor to the radiological indices. It is recommended that artisans in the DCS sector undergo mandatory radiological safety training and that wastewater treatment facilities be installed. Furthermore, regulatory agencies should encourage eco-friendly dyeing technologies. There is a need for further research on land uses where wastewater is being generated. This study can be considered as baseline data for future evaluation of the radiological impacts of different land use activities on human beings and the environment.
